input:
This staffing review takes a detailed look at the resourcing position of a maintenance crew that currently consists of 15 full-time members of staff, and which ran overtime at something like 9% of paid hours over the course of last year. The central question that the review sets out to explore is whether it might make sense to replace around half of that overtime with one additional hire, bearing in mind that an additional hire of this kind would cost in the region of $75k per year once all of the fully loaded costs are taken into account.

At first glance, the idea can look quite attractive, because overtime is often seen as something of an inefficiency that a permanent member of staff would simply absorb. However, there is a very important nuance that needs to be brought into the picture here, which is the question of timing. A new hire, once appointed, is paid for the full year, month in and month out, regardless of what the workload happens to be doing at any given moment. The overtime that this hire would be replacing, on the other hand, is not spread evenly across the year at all: instead, it is heavily concentrated into just two seasonal peaks, and outside those peaks the crew simply works its normal contracted hours. This means that, for a large part of the year, the business would effectively be paying $75k for additional capacity that the quieter months do not actually need or use. Decision-makers will therefore want to think very carefully about whether converting a cost that only arises at peak times into a fixed cost of $75k that runs all year round is really the most sensible way forward in this particular situation.
target:
A maintenance crew of 15 full-time staff ran overtime at 9% of paid hours last year. The review tests one change: replace half the overtime with one additional hire, at a fully loaded cost of $75k per year. The finding of the review is in the timing of the two arrangements, and the timing does not favour the hire on the figures given.

The trade-off is stated in one sentence: the hire costs $75k in every month of the year, while the overtime it replaces arises in two seasonal peaks and is absent between them. A hire is paid for the full year. Overtime is concentrated in the two peaks, so for most of the year the additional hire is paid to cover a load that is not there, and the capacity the hire adds is capacity the quiet months do not use. What the overtime costs at its premium rates is a separate figure and is not the figure under review here; the comparison the review makes is between a fixed year-round cost and a variable cost that arises only when the work arises.

The review therefore leaves the decision where the figures leave it. Where the peaks are long or the overtime causes failures of cover, a hire may still be the right answer on grounds outside this comparison. On cost timing alone, replacing half the overtime with one hire converts a peak-only cost into a full-year cost of $75k, and that conversion is the whole of the case against the change.
